Measurements and Units.intro: Physics describes nature with measurable quantities. A measurement is a number together with a unit; the unit gives the number meaning.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Precision, accuracy and uncertainty; Instrument choice and reading; and Dimensional checks.

The seven SI base quantities are length (m), mass (kg), time (s), electric current (A), temperature (K), amount of substance (mol) and luminous intensity (cd). Derived units come from these: velocity m s⁻¹, force newton (N = kg m s⁻²), energy joule (J = N m), pressure pascal (Pa = N m⁻²). Use prefixes such as milli = 10⁻³, micro = 10⁻⁶, kilo = 10³ and mega = 10⁶. Vernier calipers measure internal/external dimensions; a micrometer measures small thicknesses; a stopwatch measures time.
Convert to SI before substituting. For example, 72 km h⁻¹ = 72 × 1000/3600 = 20 m s⁻¹. Dimensions can test whether an equation is plausible, but do not prove it is physically correct.

A reading is never more precise than the instrument allows. Resolution is the smallest scale interval or display step; accuracy is closeness to the true value. Repeating a measurement and averaging can reduce random error, but it cannot remove a consistent zero error. Quote a result to sensible significant figures and include its unit.

Choose an instrument whose range includes the value and whose resolution is suitably small: a metre rule is not ideal for a thin wire, while a micrometer may be. For analogue scales, align the eye with the mark to avoid parallax. Check the zero before use; if the instrument reads 0.02 cm with jaws closed, correct later readings for that offset.

Write a derived quantity in base dimensions: speed [LT⁻¹], acceleration [LT⁻²], force [MLT⁻²], energy [ML²T⁻²]. Both sides of a valid equation must have the same dimensions. This catches many unit mistakes, though it cannot detect a missing numerical constant.

Scalars and Vectors.intro: Some quantities are fully described by size alone; others also require direction. This distinction changes how quantities are added.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Representing direction; Resolving a vector; and Resultant and direction.

A scalar has magnitude only: mass, time, distance, speed, energy and temperature. A vector has magnitude and direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum and electric field. Add vectors by drawing them head-to-tail or resolving them into perpendicular components. For a vector A at angle θ to the horizontal, Ax = A cos θ and Ay = A sin θ. The resultant of perpendicular components is √(Ax² + Ay²), with direction tan⁻¹(Ay/Ax).
A displacement of 3 m east followed by 4 m north gives resultant √(3² + 4²) = 5 m, at tan⁻¹(4/3) = 53.1° north of east. Distance travelled is 7 m; displacement is 5 m in a direction.

Motion.intro: Motion is a change of position with time relative to a chosen reference point. The equations of uniformly accelerated motion apply only when acceleration is constant.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Distance-time and velocity-time graphs; Choosing an equation; and Vertical motion.

Distance is total path length; displacement is directed change in position. Average speed = total distance/time; average velocity = displacement/time. Acceleration a = (v − u)/t. For constant a: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u + v)t. On a displacement-time graph, gradient is velocity. On a velocity-time graph, gradient is acceleration and signed area is displacement. Free fall near Earth has g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻² downward (often 10 m s⁻² in exam estimates).
A car accelerates uniformly from 5 m s⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹ in 4 s. a = (25−5)/4 = 5 m s⁻²; distance = average velocity × time = ½(5+25)×4 = 60 m.

On a velocity-time graph, a horizontal line means constant velocity, a rising line positive acceleration, and a falling line negative acceleration (but the object may still move forward). The four constant-acceleration equations connect u, v, a, s and t. Pick the equation that contains the requested unknown and the values supplied, rather than inserting all numbers into several formulas. If time is absent, v²=u²+2as is often convenient; if final speed is absent, s=ut+½at² may fit.

For a freely falling body close to Earth, acceleration is g downward when air resistance is negligible. Choose upward or downward as positive and keep the sign of g consistent. At the highest point of an upward throw, instantaneous velocity is zero but acceleration remains downward at g.

Gravitational Field.intro: Gravity is the attractive interaction between masses. A gravitational field describes the force that a mass would experience at each point.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Field strength and inverse-square behaviour; Mass, weight and apparent weight; and Orbits.

Field strength g = F/m and near Earth is approximately 9.8 N kg⁻¹, equivalent to 9.8 m s⁻². Weight W = mg; mass is the amount of matter and is measured in kg, while weight is a force in N and changes with g. Newton’s universal law is F = Gm₁m₂/r². Gravitational potential energy near Earth is mgh. For a circular orbit, gravity provides centripetal force; satellites farther from Earth have lower orbital speed and longer period.
A 60 kg person has weight W = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N on Earth. Their mass remains 60 kg on the Moon, but weight is smaller because lunar g is smaller.

A field is a model for action at a distance. The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass on a small test mass. For an isolated spherical body, g=GM/r² outside it, so doubling distance from the centre reduces g to one quarter. Near Earth's surface, g is nearly constant over small height changes.

Mass measures inertia and does not depend on location. Weight is gravitational force mg. In a lift accelerating upward, a scale can show a larger normal force than mg; in free fall it reads zero even though Earth's gravitational field remains. Astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they and their spacecraft are falling together.

A satellite stays in orbit because gravity supplies centripetal acceleration. In a circular orbit, GMm/r²=mv²/r, so v=√(GM/r). Increasing orbital radius lowers orbital speed. A geostationary satellite must orbit above the equator in Earth's rotation direction with a 24-hour period.

Equilibrium of Forces.intro: An object is in mechanical equilibrium when it has no linear or angular acceleration. It may be at rest or move at constant velocity.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Moments and the principle of moments; Centre of gravity and stability; and Force diagrams.

For translational equilibrium, the vector sum of forces is zero: ΣFx=0 and ΣFy=0. For rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any pivot. Moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot, measured in N m. A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces separated by a distance; its moment is one force times perpendicular separation. A body's centre of gravity is the point through which its weight acts.
A 4 N force acts 0.30 m from a pivot. Its moment is 1.2 N m. A 6 N force on the other side balances it at distance 1.2/6 = 0.20 m.
3. Moments and the principle of moments

A force can cause turning about a pivot. Moment depends on the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force's line of action, not simply the length of the object. A small force far from a pivot can balance a larger force nearby. The principle of moments applies to a body in rotational equilibrium.

The line of action of weight passes through the centre of gravity. An object is stable if a small tilt raises its centre of gravity and the vertical line through it remains within its base. A wider base and lower centre of gravity usually increase stability. If that vertical line falls outside the base, the object topples.

Draw each force at the point where it acts: weight downward, normal reaction perpendicular to the surface, tension along a taut string, and friction along the contact surface opposing impending/actual relative slip. Resolve angled forces into horizontal and vertical components before applying ΣF=0.

Work, Energy and Power.intro: Work is energy transferred when a force causes displacement. Energy is conserved, although it can change form or spread to the surroundings.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Energy transfers and conservation; Work by angled forces; and Efficiency and power.

For a constant force parallel to motion, W=Fs; at angle θ, W=Fs cosθ. Kinetic energy Ek=½mv²; gravitational potential energy near Earth Ep=mgh. Power P=W/t=ΔE/t and, for steady motion under a parallel force, P=Fv. Efficiency = useful output energy/input energy ×100%. The work-energy theorem states net work equals change in kinetic energy. A negative work term means the force removes mechanical energy, for example friction.
A 2 kg object moving at 3 m s⁻¹ has Ek=½×2×3²=9 J. Raising it 4 m adds Ep=2×9.8×4=78.4 J.

Mechanical energy may change between kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential and thermal forms. If resistive forces are negligible, total mechanical energy is conserved. With friction, mechanical energy decreases, but total energy is still conserved because energy is transferred to internal energy of the surfaces and surroundings.

Only the component of a force parallel to displacement transfers work: W=Fs cosθ. A force perpendicular to movement does zero work; a force opposing movement does negative work. For a varying force, work is the area under a force-displacement graph. Net work equals change in kinetic energy.

Power measures transfer per unit time. A machine can have high power but low efficiency; these are different ideas. Efficiency can be calculated using useful output power/input power as well as energy. In lifting at constant speed, input power at the effort is Fv, while useful output power is load×vertical speed.

Simple Machines.intro: A machine changes the size or direction of a force, or the distance over which it acts. It cannot create energy.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Mechanical advantage and velocity ratio; Levers and pulleys; and Inclined planes and gears.

Mechanical advantage MA = load/effort. Velocity ratio VR = distance moved by effort/distance moved by load. Efficiency = MA/VR ×100%. For an ideal machine, input work equals output work and MA=VR. In a lever, moments about the pivot balance; a pulley system's ideal VR equals the number of rope sections supporting the moving load. Examples include levers, pulleys, wheel-and-axle, inclined planes, screws and gears.
A machine lifts 240 N using 60 N effort. MA=4. If VR=5, efficiency=4/5×100%=80%.

Mechanical advantage compares output force (load) with input force (effort). Velocity ratio compares the distance moved by effort with the distance moved by load. Their ratio gives efficiency. The ideal machine has no friction and transfers all input work to the load, so MA=VR; an actual machine has MA<VR.

A lever balances moments: effort×effort arm = load×load arm for an ideal lever. First-class levers have pivot between effort and load; second-class have load between pivot and effort; third-class have effort between pivot and load. For a block-and-tackle, count supporting rope sections to estimate ideal velocity ratio, not the free ends of rope.

An inclined plane trades a smaller force for a longer distance. In an ideal plane, effort×length=load×height. Gears transmit rotation: a small driving gear turning a larger driven gear reduces angular speed but increases torque, ideally conserving power.

Friction.intro: Friction is a contact force that opposes relative motion or its tendency between surfaces. It can be useful for walking and braking, but it dissipates mechanical energy as heat.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Static friction and motion onset; Friction on a slope; and Useful and harmful effects.

Static friction adjusts up to a limiting value; kinetic/sliding friction acts during sliding. In the simple model, limiting friction Fmax=μR, where μ is the coefficient of friction and R is the normal reaction. Friction depends on surface materials and normal force; the model often treats it as independent of apparent contact area. Lubrication, polishing, ball bearings and streamlining reduce different kinds of resistance.
If μ=0.25 and R=80 N, limiting friction is 0.25×80=20 N. A 12 N pull can be balanced by 12 N static friction; motion does not start yet.

Static friction is self-adjusting: it matches the applied tangential force until reaching a maximum μsR. An object can therefore be pushed gently without moving. Once it begins to slide, kinetic friction is commonly modelled as μkR and is often smaller than the limiting static friction. The coefficient has no unit and depends on the pair of surfaces.

On an inclined plane, resolve weight into components: mg sinθ down the slope and mg cosθ perpendicular to it. If no other perpendicular force acts, R=mg cosθ. Friction acts along the surface and opposes actual or impending relative motion. A block sliding down a slope may have friction acting up the slope.

Friction provides grip for walking, tyre traction and braking; it also produces heat and wear. Lubricants separate surfaces, rolling elements replace sliding friction, and streamlined shapes reduce fluid drag. Reducing friction is not always safe: tyres and shoe soles need adequate grip.

Elasticity.intro: Elasticity is the ability of a material to regain its original shape after a deforming force is removed. Deformation beyond the elastic limit may be permanent.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Force-extension behaviour; Stress and strain; and Energy stored.

Hooke’s law states extension is proportional to applied force while the elastic limit is not exceeded: F=kx, where k is stiffness in N m⁻¹. Stress=force/cross-sectional area (Pa); strain=extension/original length (dimensionless). Young modulus E=stress/strain. Elastic potential energy in a spring is ½kx², equal to the area under a straight-line force-extension graph.
A spring extends 0.04 m under 8 N. k=8/0.04=200 N m⁻¹. At this extension its stored energy is ½×200×0.04²=0.16 J.

A force-extension graph begins as a straight line for a Hookean spring; gradient is stiffness k. When the graph curves, extension is no longer proportional to force. The elastic limit marks the greatest deformation from which a specimen fully returns to its original shape; beyond it, permanent deformation may remain.

Stress measures internal force per unit area, while strain measures fractional change in length. A thin wire experiences greater stress than a thick wire for the same load. Young modulus describes stiffness of a material and is the gradient of a stress-strain graph in the elastic region. It is not the same as spring constant, which depends on both material and shape.

The elastic energy stored is the area under the force-extension graph. For a Hookean spring it is ½Fx=½kx². If a force-extension graph is not straight, use its area rather than applying the triangular formula. On unloading, a hysteresis loop indicates energy dissipated internally.

Pressure.intro: Pressure measures force distributed over an area. The same force produces greater pressure on a smaller area.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Pressure in solids and fluids; Hydraulic systems; and Pressure measurement.

Pressure p=F/A, in pascals (Pa = N m⁻²). In a fluid at rest, pressure acts in all directions. For a liquid of density ρ at depth h, gauge pressure p=ρgh; absolute pressure adds atmospheric pressure. Pressure transmission in an enclosed fluid underlies hydraulic devices (Pascal’s principle). A barometer measures atmospheric pressure; a manometer compares gas pressure with a reference pressure.
A 200 N force acts on area 0.04 m². p=200/0.04=5000 Pa.

For a solid, pressure is the normal force divided by contact area. A sharp blade has a small area and therefore a large pressure; broad snowshoes spread a person's weight over a larger area. In a fluid, pressure at a point acts in every direction, and a confined pressure increase is transmitted throughout the fluid.

Pascal's principle allows a small force on a small piston to produce a larger force on a large piston: F₁/A₁=F₂/A₂. The larger force comes with a smaller output distance; ideally the input and output work are equal. Hydraulic brakes use fluid to transmit force to multiple wheels.

A manometer uses a column of liquid: pressure difference Δp=ρgh for vertical level difference h. A barometer supports a column whose height balances atmospheric pressure. In gas problems, state whether pressure is absolute or gauge; absolute pressure is gauge pressure plus atmospheric pressure.

Liquids at Rest.intro: A liquid at rest exerts pressure on the walls and bottom of its container. Pressure grows with depth because deeper layers support more liquid above them.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Buoyancy and Archimedes' principle; Floating, sinking and density; and Pressure and connected liquids.

Hydrostatic pressure p=ρgh. Upthrust is the resultant upward force from the pressure difference between the bottom and top of an immersed body. Archimedes’ principle: upthrust equals the weight of displaced fluid. An object floats when upthrust balances its weight; its average density is then less than the liquid's density. For a floating body, fraction submerged ≈ object density/liquid density. Communicating vessels settle at equal levels when exposed to the same pressure.
A 0.002 m³ object is fully immersed in water. Upthrust=ρgV=1000×9.8×0.002=19.6 N.

Pressure increases with depth, creating a larger upward pressure force on the lower surface than downward force on the upper surface. The net upthrust equals the weight of displaced liquid. A fully submerged object displaces a volume equal to its own volume; a floating body displaces only enough liquid to balance its weight.

An object sinks if its weight exceeds the maximum available upthrust; it rises if upthrust is greater. In equilibrium while floating, upthrust=weight. Therefore, submerged fraction is object density/fluid density for a uniform floating object. A steel ship floats because its hollow shape makes its average density, including enclosed air, less than water.

At equal depths in the same connected liquid, pressure is equal. A U-tube manometer compares pressure by balancing liquid columns; for the same liquid, Δp=ρgΔh. If columns contain different liquids, equate pressures at a common horizontal level using each density and height.

Temperature and Its Measurement.intro: Temperature indicates how hot or cold a body is and determines the direction of net thermal energy transfer. It is not the same as heat energy.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Thermometric properties; Fixed points and scales; and Choosing a thermometer.

Thermometers use a thermometric property that changes reproducibly, such as liquid volume, electrical resistance or thermocouple voltage. Celsius and Kelvin scales are related by T(K)=θ(°C)+273.15. For a linear scale, θ=(X−X₀)/(X₁−X₀)×100°C between ice and steam points. Clinical thermometers have a narrow range; laboratory thermometers usually do not have a constriction. Absolute zero is 0 K (−273.15°C).
A temperature of 27°C is 300.15 K, approximately 300 K. A change of 1°C equals a change of 1 K.

A thermometer works because a physical property changes with temperature. Liquid-in-glass thermometers use volume; resistance thermometers use electrical resistance; thermocouples use an emf. A good thermometric property changes steadily and reproducibly over the required range. Calibration compares the property at known fixed points and assigns scale readings.

On the Celsius scale, ice point is 0°C and steam point is 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure. A linear thermometer can be calibrated by interpolating between its readings X₀ and X₁ at these points. Kelvin starts at absolute zero and is the thermodynamic scale; temperature differences have the same numerical size in kelvin and degrees Celsius.

A clinical thermometer has a narrow range around body temperature and often a constriction to retain the maximum reading. A laboratory thermometer has a wider range and should be read while its bulb remains in the substance. A thermocouple responds quickly and can measure high temperatures.

Thermal Expansion.intro: Most materials expand when heated because their particles vibrate more strongly and their average separation increases. Expansion matters in bridges, railway tracks, pipes and thermometers.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Expansion of solids, liquids and gases; Practical design; and Water's anomaly.

For small temperature changes, linear expansion ΔL=αL₀ΔT; area expansion is approximately 2αA₀ΔT and volume expansion approximately 3αV₀ΔT for isotropic solids. α is the coefficient of linear expansion in K⁻¹. Liquids show apparent expansion because both liquid and container expand; anomalous expansion of water occurs between 0°C and 4°C, with maximum density at 4°C. Bimetallic strips bend because their metals have different α values.
A 2 m metal rod with α=1.2×10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ is heated by 50 K. ΔL=1.2×10⁻⁵×2×50=0.0012 m =1.2 mm.
3. Expansion of solids, liquids and gases

Heating usually increases average particle separation in solids and liquids; gases expand more because particles are much farther apart and intermolecular attractions are weaker. For an isotropic solid, area expansion coefficient is about twice the linear coefficient and volume expansion coefficient about three times it for small temperature changes.

Bridges use expansion joints, railway tracks have gaps, and long pipelines need bends or sliding supports. Overhead wires sag more on hot days. Bimetallic strips bend because one metal expands more; thermostats use this bending to open or close a circuit. A rigidly constrained expansion can generate large compressive stress.

Water contracts as it cools from high temperature to 4°C, then expands as it cools from 4°C to freezing. Ice is therefore less dense and floats. In a lake, surface water freezes first; the ice layer insulates the liquid below, helping aquatic organisms survive.

Quantity of Heat.intro: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. A body's temperature change depends on its mass, material and heat capacity.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Specific heat capacity; Calorimetry; and Electrical heating method.

For a temperature change without change of state, Q=mcΔT, where c is specific heat capacity in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Heat capacity C=Q/ΔT=mc. In calorimetry, energy lost by hotter bodies equals energy gained by cooler bodies in an insulated system. Electrical heating energy can be found from Q=VIt=I²Rt. Some energy may escape to the surroundings, so measured values can differ from ideal predictions.
Heating 0.50 kg of water by 20 K needs Q=0.50×4200×20=42,000 J.

Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 K without changing state. A high c means a large energy input produces a relatively small temperature rise. In an insulated mixture, heat lost by the hotter object equals heat gained by the cooler one, assuming no phase change or reaction. Include the container's heat capacity if it is not negligible. A calorimeter reduces, but does not eliminate, transfer to the surroundings; practical results may be corrected for such losses.

Change of State.intro: Matter changes between solid, liquid and gas when energy changes particle arrangement and separation. During a pure substance's phase change at fixed pressure, temperature remains constant while latent heat is transferred.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Heating curves; Latent heats and staged calculations; and Evaporation and boiling.

Specific latent heat L=Q/m, so Q=mL. Latent heat of fusion changes solid to liquid; latent heat of vaporization changes liquid to gas. The heating curve has sloping sections (temperature changes; Q=mcΔT) and flat sections (state changes; Q=mL). Melting and freezing, boiling and condensation are reverse processes. Evaporation occurs at the surface below boiling point and causes cooling; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling point.
Melting 0.20 kg of ice at 0°C requires Q=mLf=0.20×3.34×10⁵=6.68×10⁴ J.

A heating curve has rising segments where temperature increases within one state and plateaus where a phase change occurs. The plateau temperature depends on pressure. During melting or boiling, supplied energy overcomes intermolecular attractions and changes potential energy; average kinetic energy and temperature remain approximately constant.

A full heating problem can involve several stages: warm a solid with mcΔT, melt it with mLf, warm the liquid, vaporize it with mLv, then warm the gas. Calculate each stage separately and add. Use the correct specific heat capacity and latent heat for each material and phase.

Evaporation occurs at the surface at temperatures below boiling because some particles have enough energy to escape. Higher-energy particles leave, so the remaining liquid cools. Boiling occurs throughout the liquid when its vapour pressure equals external pressure. Lower external pressure lowers the boiling point.

Vapours.intro: A vapour is the gaseous form of a substance that is normally liquid or solid under the stated conditions. Evaporation and condensation establish vapour pressure in a closed space.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Saturated vapour and dynamic equilibrium; Humidity and dew point; and Boiling and external pressure.

Saturated vapour is in dynamic equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature; its pressure is the saturated vapour pressure. Vapour pressure rises with temperature. Relative humidity = actual water-vapour pressure/saturated vapour pressure at that temperature ×100%. Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated as it cools. Evaporation is faster with greater exposed area, higher temperature, moving air and lower humidity. Boiling occurs when vapour pressure equals external pressure.
If actual vapour pressure is 1.2 kPa and saturation pressure is 2.0 kPa, relative humidity=60%.

In a closed container above a liquid, evaporation continues while some vapour molecules condense. At equilibrium the rates are equal; the vapour is saturated. At a fixed temperature, saturated vapour pressure is characteristic of the liquid. Warming increases the fraction of molecules able to escape and raises vapour pressure.

Relative humidity compares actual vapour pressure with saturation pressure at the same temperature. Cooling air without removing water raises relative humidity; when it reaches 100%, condensation begins. The dew point is that temperature. Dew, mist and clouds form when water vapour condenses on surfaces or particles.

A liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure reaches external pressure. A pressure cooker raises the external pressure, so water boils above 100°C and food cooks faster. At high altitude, pressure is lower, so water boils below 100°C and cooking may take longer.

Structure of Matter and Kinetic Theory.intro: The kinetic model explains observable properties using particles in motion. Solids, liquids and gases differ mainly in particle arrangement, separation and freedom of movement.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Particle arrangements; Pressure and temperature microscopically; and Diffusion and Brownian motion.

In a solid, particles vibrate about fixed positions; in a liquid they remain close but move past one another; in a gas they move rapidly and randomly with large separations. Gas pressure results from molecular collisions with container walls. For an ideal gas, mean translational kinetic energy per molecule is proportional to absolute temperature. Diffusion is net spreading from high to low concentration and is faster at higher temperature; it is generally faster in gases than liquids.
At constant volume, doubling absolute temperature doubles the mean kinetic energy per molecule. A Celsius value must be converted to kelvin for gas relationships.

Solids have close-packed particles with fixed mean positions; liquids have close particles that rearrange; gases have widely separated particles moving freely. These models account for shape, volume, compressibility and diffusion. A gas is easily compressed because most of its volume is empty space between particles.

Gas pressure comes from momentum change during collisions with container walls. Increasing temperature at fixed volume increases mean molecular speed and collision force/frequency, raising pressure. At fixed pressure, a heated gas expands so its particles can travel farther between wall collisions. Absolute zero is the theoretical limit at which classical translational motion has minimum energy.

Diffusion is net movement down a concentration gradient caused by random particle motion. Brownian motion is the irregular movement of visible particles due to unbalanced collisions with much smaller molecules; it provides evidence for molecular motion. Increasing temperature makes both the molecular motion and diffusion rate greater.

Heat Transfer.intro: Thermal energy moves from a hotter region to a cooler one by conduction, convection or radiation. In practice, more than one method may act at once.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Comparing the three methods; Conduction and insulation; and Convection and radiation control.

Conduction transfers energy through particle interactions without bulk movement of the material; metals conduct well because mobile electrons transport energy. Convection transfers energy by bulk motion in fluids: heated, less-dense fluid rises and cooler fluid replaces it. Radiation is electromagnetic (mainly infrared) and needs no medium. Dull black surfaces are good absorbers and emitters; shiny light surfaces are poor absorbers and emitters. Insulation reduces one or more transfer routes.

Gas Laws.intro: Gas laws relate pressure, volume and temperature for a fixed amount of gas. They describe ideal gases approximately when molecules are far apart and intermolecular forces are small.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Boyle's law; Charles' and pressure laws; and Moles and ideal behaviour.

Boyle’s law: pV=constant at fixed temperature. Charles’ law: V/T=constant at fixed pressure. Pressure law: p/T=constant at fixed volume. Combined gas law: p₁V₁/T₁=p₂V₂/T₂. Ideal gas equation pV=nRT. Always use absolute temperature in kelvin and consistent units; R=8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The laws follow from molecular collisions and average kinetic energy.
A gas at 300 K occupies 2.0 L at constant pressure. At 450 K, V₂=2.0×450/300=3.0 L.

For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, reducing volume makes molecules hit the walls more frequently per unit area and pressure rises: pV remains constant. A p-versus-V graph is a curve; a p-versus-1/V graph is a straight line. This law describes slow compression that allows temperature to remain constant.

At constant pressure, heating a gas increases its volume in proportion to kelvin temperature. At constant volume, pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature. A graph against Celsius does not pass through zero; extrapolation reaches −273.15°C, absolute zero, in the ideal model.

The ideal gas equation combines pV=nRT. It works best at low pressure and high temperature, when particles are far apart and attractions matter less. At high pressure or near condensation, real gases deviate because particles occupy volume and attract one another. Convert volume to m³ if using R=8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ with pressure in Pa.

Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to travel; longitudinal waves oscillate parallel to travel and contain compressions and rarefactions. Amplitude is maximum displacement; wavelength λ is distance between matching points; frequency f is oscillations per second; period T=1/f. Wave speed v=fλ. Reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference describe common wave behaviours. In refraction, frequency remains fixed while speed and wavelength may change.

Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength. For a stationary wave, nodes have zero displacement and adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength.

Reflection returns a wave into its original medium. Refraction changes direction and speed at a boundary; diffraction is spreading through an opening or around an obstacle, most noticeable when its size is similar to wavelength. Superposition adds displacements; constructive and destructive interference can form patterns.

For transverse waves, the vibration is at right angles to travel; examples include light and waves on a string. For longitudinal waves, vibration is parallel to travel; sound in air has compressions and rarefactions. Waves transfer energy, but particles oscillate around equilibrium rather than travelling with the wave overall.

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Sound production and transmission; Measuring sound speed; and Ultrasound and applications.

In air, sound is longitudinal, travelling through compressions and rarefactions. The source sets frequency; the medium determines speed. Speed is greater in most solids than liquids and gases. An echo is reflected sound; distance to a reflecting surface = vt/2 because the sound travels to the surface and back. Ultrasound has frequency above about 20 kHz and is used in imaging and ranging; infrasound is below 20 Hz.
An echo returns after 0.40 s; with sound speed 340 m s⁻¹, wall distance=340×0.40/2=68 m.

A vibrating source pushes nearby particles together and then lets them spread, creating compressions and rarefactions. Each particle oscillates about its equilibrium position and passes the disturbance onward. Sound speed depends on the medium's elasticity and density; it is usually faster in solids because restoring forces are strong.

In a time-of-flight experiment, measure a known distance and time the sound path; repeat and average. For an echo, use round-trip time and divide distance by two. In air, temperature affects sound speed, so use the value supplied or suitable conditions rather than treating 340 m s⁻¹ as universal.

Ultrasound can be reflected at boundaries between tissues or materials. A scanner measures echo time and uses the known speed to infer depth. SONAR uses the same principle underwater. High-frequency sound is more directional but may be absorbed more strongly; couplants improve transmission between a probe and the body.

Characteristics of Sound Waves.intro: The pitch, loudness and quality of a sound relate to different physical features of its wave. These terms should not be interchanged.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Frequency, amplitude and pitch; Timbre and overtones; and Resonance and hearing.

Pitch depends mainly on frequency: higher frequency sounds higher. Loudness depends on intensity and is related to amplitude; intensity is power per unit area and approximately falls as 1/r² from a point source. Quality or timbre depends on waveform and overtones, allowing instruments to sound different at the same pitch and loudness. The decibel scale is logarithmic. Resonance occurs when a driving frequency matches a natural frequency and produces a large response.
If distance from a point source doubles, intensity becomes approximately one quarter, assuming no absorption or reflecting boundaries.

The source vibration frequency determines the sound's pitch. The wave amplitude is related to intensity, but perceived loudness also depends on frequency and the listener's hearing. Sound intensity is power per area and falls with distance for a point source in open space. The ear's response is logarithmic, which is why decibels are used.

A musical note usually contains a fundamental frequency and overtones. The mix and relative strength of these components shape the waveform and timbre. Two instruments can play the same fundamental note at equal loudness but still sound different because their harmonic content differs.

A system resonates when driven near a natural frequency, so it absorbs energy efficiently and oscillation amplitude grows. Resonance can amplify sound in an instrument's body or cause unwanted vibration in structures. The audible range for a young human is approximately 20 Hz to 20 kHz, but it varies with age and individual hearing.

Light Energy.intro: Light is electromagnetic radiation visible to the human eye. It travels in straight lines in a uniform medium and can be reflected, refracted, absorbed or transmitted.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Ray model and shadows; Sources and illumination; and Light speed and time.

In vacuum, light speed c≈3.0×10⁸ m s⁻¹. A ray is a model showing direction of propagation; a beam is a collection of rays. Luminous objects emit light; non-luminous objects are seen by reflected light. Transparent materials transmit a clear image, translucent materials scatter light, and opaque materials do not transmit it. Shadows form when opaque objects block rays. The eye focuses light on the retina; rods and cones respond to light.
Light from a lamp travels in straight lines through uniform air; an opaque object produces a region of umbra and, for an extended source, penumbra.

A ray model represents the direction light travels; it is useful when wavelength effects are negligible. A point source forms a sharp shadow, while an extended source produces a dark umbra and a partial penumbra. Transparent media transmit light regularly; translucent media scatter it; opaque media absorb or reflect it without transmitting through.

Luminous sources produce their own light; illuminated objects are seen because they reflect or scatter light. Light intensity from a point source in free space approximately follows an inverse-square law. Surface colour depends on wavelengths reflected into the eye and on the illumination spectrum.

Light travels at about 3.0×10⁸ m s⁻¹ in vacuum. It slows in material media; refractive index relates vacuum speed to medium speed. The finite speed matters in astronomy and communication: looking at distant objects means seeing light that left them earlier.

Reflection of Light at Plane and Curved.intro: Reflection changes the direction of light at a surface. Plane mirrors form virtual upright images; curved mirrors can form real or virtual images depending on object position.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

Law of reflection: angle of incidence i equals angle of reflection r, measured from the normal. A plane mirror image is virtual, upright, same size, laterally inverted and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Concave mirrors converge parallel rays; convex mirrors diverge them. For spherical mirrors, f=R/2 and mirror equation 1/f=1/u+1/v under the chosen sign convention; magnification m=image height/object height=v/u (sign indicates orientation under convention).
An object 2 m in front of a plane mirror has its image 2 m behind it, so object-image separation is 4 m.

Refraction of Light.intro: Refraction is the change in direction of light when it crosses a boundary at which its speed changes. A ray entering a more optically dense medium bends toward the normal.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Refractive index and bending; Critical angle and total internal reflection; and Apparent depth and lenses.

Refractive index n=c/v and Snell’s law n₁sin i=n₂sin r. Frequency stays constant at the boundary, while speed and wavelength change. A ray entering a slower medium bends toward the normal; leaving it bends away. At the critical angle c for light travelling from denser to rarer medium, refracted angle is 90° and sin c=n₂/n₁. Total internal reflection requires incidence angle greater than c and travel from higher to lower refractive index; optical fibres use this effect.
For air to glass with n≈1.5, sin c=1/1.5, so c≈41.8°.

If the ray enters along the normal, its speed changes but its direction does not.

For light going from index n₁ to lower n₂, at the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the boundary. Above this angle all light is reflected internally. This requires travel from denser to rarer optical medium. A fibre's core has higher refractive index than its cladding so rays reflect repeatedly and remain guided.

A submerged object appears closer to the surface because rays bend away from the normal on leaving water. For near-normal viewing, apparent depth ≈ real depth/refractive index. This effect, together with lens refraction, underlies many optical instruments.

Optical Instruments.intro: Optical instruments use lenses or mirrors to form images that help the eye see small, distant or otherwise inaccessible objects.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Lens image formation; Microscopes and telescopes; and Eye defects and correction.

A converging lens brings parallel rays to its principal focus; a diverging lens spreads them. Thin-lens equation 1/f=1/u+1/v (use the course sign convention); linear magnification m=image height/object height. A simple microscope uses a converging lens with the object inside its focal length to produce an enlarged virtual image. A compound microscope uses objective and eyepiece lenses. A telescope uses an objective to form an image of a distant object and an eyepiece to magnify it. The eye accommodates by changing lens curvature; short-sightedness is corrected with a diverging lens and long-sightedness with a converging lens.
A lens with f=10 cm has object distance u=15 cm. Using the real-is-positive school convention, 1/v=1/10−1/15=1/30, so v=30 cm.

A converging lens can make a real image when the object is beyond its focal length; the image can be caught on a screen. When the object is inside the focal length, the image is virtual, upright and enlarged. A diverging lens forms a virtual, upright, diminished image for a real object. Ray diagrams reveal orientation and whether an image is real.

A compound microscope's objective forms a magnified real intermediate image; the eyepiece acts as a magnifier. A telescope's objective forms an image of a distant object near its focal plane; the eyepiece magnifies the angle it subtends. Larger objective aperture gathers more light and can improve resolution.

The eye lens focuses images on the retina. Myopia focuses distant images in front of the retina and is corrected by a diverging lens; hyperopia tends to focus near images behind the retina and is corrected by a converging lens. Accommodation changes lens curvature for near and far objects.

Dispersion of Light and Colours.intro: White light contains a range of visible wavelengths. Dispersion occurs when refractive index varies with wavelength, separating the colours.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Prism spectrum; Rainbows and colour mixing; and Objects, filters and illumination.

A prism refracts different wavelengths by different amounts; violet is generally deviated more than red in glass. The visible spectrum order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. A rainbow forms through refraction, dispersion and internal reflection in water droplets. Colour of an opaque object depends on the wavelengths it reflects and the illumination; a filter transmits selected wavelengths and absorbs others.
A red object under white light reflects red strongly and absorbs much of the other visible light. Under blue-only illumination it may appear dark because little red light is available to reflect.

A prism's non-parallel faces refract light on entry and exit. Refractive index varies with wavelength, so colours bend by different amounts. In ordinary glass violet deviates more than red. A single refracting surface may spread colours slightly, but the prism geometry makes the separation visible as a spectrum.

Sunlight is refracted and dispersed on entering raindrops, internally reflected, and refracted again on exit. Different wavelengths leave at different angles. Red, green and blue are additive primary colours of light; combining them appropriately can produce white. Pigment mixing is subtractive because pigments absorb selected wavelengths.

A red filter transmits mainly red wavelengths and absorbs others. A white object reflects most visible wavelengths; a black object absorbs most. An object does not carry a fixed visible colour independent of light: a green object illuminated only by red light may look dark.

Electrostatics.intro: Electrostatics concerns electric charge at rest. Charge is conserved and occurs in positive and negative forms; like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Charging and induction; Electric field patterns; and Coulomb force.

An electron carries −e, a proton +e; e=1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C. Charging by friction transfers electrons; conduction transfers charge through contact; induction redistributes charge without contact. Coulomb’s law F=kq₁q₂/r² in vacuum. Electric field strength E=F/q; for a point charge E=kQ/r². Electric field lines point away from positive and toward negative charge; they never cross. A conductor permits mobile charge movement; an insulator does not readily.
Two charges each 2 μC separated by 0.30 m repel with F≈9×10⁹(2×10⁻⁶)²/(0.30)²=0.40 N.

Frictional charging occurs when electrons move between materials; the total charge of an isolated system remains conserved. In a conductor, charges redistribute until the conductor is at one potential. Bringing a charged object nearby separates charge in a neutral conductor; grounding can allow electrons to enter or leave, leaving a net charge after the ground is removed.

Field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges or extend to infinity. The tangent gives field direction, and line density indicates relative strength. Between parallel plates the field is nearly uniform away from edges. A charged particle in a uniform field experiences F=qE; a negative charge feels force opposite to field direction.

Coulomb's law has inverse-square dependence and acts along the line joining point charges. Like-charge force is repulsive; unlike-charge force is attractive. In a system with several charges, calculate each force direction and use vector addition for the resultant. The force on charge q is related to the field created by other charges, not its own field.

Capacitors.intro: A capacitor stores separated charge and electric-field energy. Its capacitance describes how much charge it stores per unit potential difference.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Charge, voltage and capacitance; Capacitor networks; and Charging and discharging.

C=Q/V, measured in farads (F). A parallel-plate capacitor has C=εA/d for ideal plates; inserting a dielectric increases capacitance. In parallel, capacitances add; in series, reciprocals add. Stored energy U=½CV²=½QV=Q²/(2C). In a charging circuit with resistor R, time constant τ=RC; charge rises toward its maximum and current decays exponentially. Capacitors smooth supply variations, store energy briefly and couple changing signals.
A 200 μF capacitor at 12 V stores Q=CV=2.4×10⁻³ C and energy U=½CV²=0.0144 J.

Capacitance depends on conductor geometry and the insulating medium, not simply on the charge currently stored. For a fixed capacitor, Q is proportional to V. A dielectric polarizes in the field, reducing effective field for a given free charge and allowing more charge at the same voltage.

In parallel, plates share the same voltage and total stored charge is the sum, so Ctotal is the sum. In series, each capacitor carries equal charge and voltage divides, so reciprocal capacitances add. A capacitor can block steady DC after charging while passing changing signals; this is useful for coupling and filtering.

Through a resistor, capacitor voltage changes exponentially with time constant RC. After one time constant during charging, voltage reaches about 63% of its final value; after about five, it is nearly fully charged. Discharge current flows in the opposite direction to charging current.

Electric Cells.intro: An electric cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy and maintains a potential difference. A real cell has internal resistance, so its terminal voltage changes under load.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Cell emf and terminal potential difference; Cells in combination; and Battery chemistry and care.

Electromotive force ε is energy supplied per unit charge around the complete circuit. For a cell delivering current I, terminal voltage V=ε−Ir, where r is internal resistance; at zero current, terminal voltage equals ε. Cells in series add emfs when oriented alike; parallel cells with equal emf increase available capacity/current capability but do not add emf. Primary cells are not rechargeable; secondary cells are designed for recharging.
A 1.5 V cell with internal resistance 0.2 Ω delivers 2 A. Terminal voltage V=1.5−(2×0.2)=1.1 V.
3. Cell emf and terminal potential difference

Emf is the energy supplied per coulomb by the source; it is not the terminal voltage under every condition. When a cell supplies current, some voltage is lost across its internal resistance. When current is zero, terminal voltage equals emf in the ideal measurement. A short-circuited cell can deliver a large unsafe current limited mainly by internal resistance.

Cells in series with like orientation add emf, but their internal resistances also add. Opposed cells subtract. Identical cells in parallel keep approximately the same emf while reducing effective internal resistance and sharing load current. Unequal emf cells should not be connected in parallel casually because circulating current may flow.

Primary cells are intended for one discharge; secondary cells can be recharged by driving current in the reverse chemical direction. Battery capacity is often quoted in ampere-hours, a charge measure, not energy. Energy also depends on voltage: watt-hours≈voltage×ampere-hours.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Domestic energy use; Fuses, earthing and safety; and Power in resistive devices.

P=VI. With Ohm’s law, P=I²R=V²/R. Energy E=Pt=VIt, measured in joules; household electrical energy is often billed in kilowatt-hours (1 kWh=3.6×10⁶ J). Fuse rating should exceed normal operating current but remain low enough to break an unsafe overload. A fuse is connected in the live wire in standard installations; earthing provides a low-resistance fault path.
A 60 W lamp used for 5 h consumes 0.060×5=0.30 kWh =1.08×10⁶ J.

An electricity meter records energy, commonly in kWh. One kilowatt-hour is the energy used by a 1 kW device in one hour, equal to 3.6 MJ. Cost is energy in kWh multiplied by the tariff. A high-power appliance used briefly can consume less energy than a low-power device left on for a long time.

A fuse melts when current exceeds its rating and is placed in the live conductor so the appliance is disconnected from the supply. Earthing connects exposed metal casing to ground with a low-resistance path; a fault current then helps operate fuse/breaker. Double-insulated appliances use two insulation layers and may not need an earth wire.

Electrical power P=VI. Combining with Ohm's law gives I²R or V²/R. A heater's resistance changes with temperature, so rated voltage and power are the best values for normal operation. Transmission at high voltage reduces current for a given power and therefore reduces I²R losses in cables.

Magnets and Magnetic Fields.intro: A magnetic field is the region where a magnetic pole or moving charge experiences magnetic force. Magnetic poles occur in north-south pairs.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Field patterns and magnetic materials; Domains and magnetization; and Earth's field.

Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Outside a bar magnet, field lines go from north to south; closer lines indicate stronger field. A compass aligns with the local field. Earth has a magnetic field, so a compass points approximately north-south. Magnetic materials include iron, cobalt and nickel; soft iron is easily magnetized and demagnetized, while steel retains magnetism more strongly. Domain alignment explains magnetization.
A plotting compass placed around a bar magnet turns tangent to a field line; reversing the magnet reverses the field direction.

A compass needle is a small magnet that aligns with the local magnetic field. Plotting compasses around a bar magnet reveal curved lines from north to south outside. A uniform field has parallel, equally spaced lines. Soft iron magnetizes and demagnetizes readily; steel is harder to magnetize but retains magnetism.

Ferromagnetic materials contain regions called domains in which atomic magnetic moments align. An unmagnetized object has domains pointing in varied directions; an external field can align many domains, producing a net field. Heating or hammering can disrupt alignment. A coil around a soft-iron core forms an electromagnet whose strength increases with current and turns.

Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor in.intro: A current-carrying conductor experiences a force when it is placed in a magnetic field because its moving charges interact with the field.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Direction of motor force; Coils and turning effect; and Loudspeakers.

For a straight conductor perpendicular to a uniform field, F=BIL; at angle θ, F=BIL sinθ. B is magnetic flux density in tesla, I current, and L conductor length within the field. Force direction follows Fleming’s left-hand rule: first finger field (N to S), second conventional current, thumb force/motion. Reversing current or field reverses force. A coil experiences a turning moment, the basis of an electric motor and loudspeaker.
A 0.20 m wire carries 3 A perpendicular to a 0.50 T field. F=0.50×3×0.20=0.30 N.

The magnetic field of the current interacts with the external field and produces a force. Fleming's left-hand rule links field, conventional current and force. Reversing either field or current reverses the force; reversing both leaves force direction unchanged. The rule predicts direction, while F=BILsinθ gives magnitude.

For a rectangular coil, forces on opposite sides act in opposite directions at different positions and create a turning moment. A split-ring commutator reverses current every half-turn so the coil continues rotating in the same rotational direction. Brushes maintain electrical contact as the coil turns. This is the DC motor principle.

An alternating audio current in a coil within a permanent magnetic field experiences an alternating force. The attached cone vibrates and creates sound waves. Increasing signal amplitude increases force and sound amplitude; frequency determines the rate of vibration and hence pitch.

Electromagnetic Induction.intro: Electromagnetic induction produces an emf when magnetic flux linking a conductor or coil changes. A current flows only if the circuit is closed.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Changing flux linkage; Lenz's law and energy; and Generators and transformers.

Faraday’s law: induced emf magnitude is proportional to rate of change of flux linkage, ε=−NΔΦ/Δt. Magnetic flux Φ=BA cosθ for a uniform field and plane coil. Lenz’s law gives the minus sign: induced current creates a field opposing the change that produced it, conserving energy. Increase induced emf by moving magnet/coil faster, using a stronger field, increasing turns or area. Generators convert mechanical energy to electrical energy.
A 100-turn coil has flux per turn changing by 0.02 Wb in 0.5 s. |ε|=NΔΦ/Δt=100×0.02/0.5=4 V.

Magnetic flux measures field passing through an area: Φ=BAcosθ for uniform B. Flux linkage is NΦ for N turns. An induced emf appears whenever this linkage changes, whether by moving the coil, changing field strength, rotating the coil or changing its area. A stationary coil in a steady field has no induced emf.

The induced current produces a field that opposes the change in flux. If a magnet is pushed toward a coil, the coil's near face becomes a pole that repels it; work must be done to push the magnet, supplying the electrical energy. This opposition is a consequence of energy conservation.

A rotating coil in a magnetic field has changing flux and produces alternating emf. A slip-ring generator gives AC; a split-ring commutator gives pulsating DC. A transformer uses changing current in a primary coil to create changing flux in a core and induce emf in a secondary; it requires AC or changing current.

Inductance.intro: Inductance describes how strongly a changing current in a circuit induces an emf that opposes the change. An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Self-induction; RL time response; and Magnetic energy.

Self-induced emf ε=−L(dI/dt); inductance L is measured in henries (H). Energy stored in an ideal inductor is U=½LI². A coil's inductance increases with turns and magnetic-core permeability and depends on geometry. In an RL circuit, current does not change instantaneously; time constant τ=L/R. Inductors oppose rapid current changes and are used in filters, transformers and ignition systems.
An inductor of 0.5 H carries 2 A. Stored energy U=½×0.5×2²=1 J.

When current in a coil changes, its magnetic field and flux linkage change, inducing an emf in the same coil. This back emf opposes the current change. When current is switched on, it delays the rise; when switched off, it can create a large voltage spike as the field collapses. A flyback diode can protect switching electronics from that spike.

In a series RL circuit, current rises toward its steady value with time constant L/R. After one time constant it has reached about 63% of final value. When the supply is removed, current decays exponentially. A larger inductance slows current change; a larger resistance shortens the time constant.

An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field, U=½LI². Energy can be returned to the circuit when the field collapses. Ignition coils exploit rapid current interruption to produce a high induced voltage; inductors also smooth current in power supplies.

Eddy Current.intro: Eddy currents are circulating currents induced within a bulk conductor when magnetic flux through it changes. They can cause heating and magnetic drag.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: How eddy currents form; Reducing unwanted effects; and Useful applications.

Changing flux induces closed loops of current inside a solid conductor; Lenz’s law makes their magnetic effects oppose the change. Laminating a transformer core breaks large current loops and reduces energy loss. Eddy currents are useful in induction cookers, electromagnetic braking and metal detectors, but unwanted in transformer cores. Slotted or laminated conductors reduce them.
A spinning aluminium disc slows when moved between magnet poles because induced eddy currents produce a magnetic force opposing its motion.

A changing magnetic flux through parts of a solid conductor induces circulating loops of current within it. Each loop creates its own magnetic field opposing the change. Moving a conductor through a magnetic field also changes flux in its material, producing eddy currents and a drag force.

Transformer cores are built from thin insulated laminations. Each sheet interrupts large current loops and increases their resistance, reducing heating and wasted energy. Slits in a conductor similarly restrict loops. The losses become more significant with changing fields and thick, highly conductive cores.

Eddy-current brakes slow trains and exercise equipment without physical contact; the braking effect grows with speed and disappears as motion stops. Induction cookers create currents in a metal pan, heating it. Eddy-current testing can detect cracks because a flaw changes the induced-current pattern.

Simple A.C. Circuits.intro: Alternating current changes direction periodically. In a simple AC circuit, resistance, capacitance and inductance affect current and voltage differently.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Alternating waveform and RMS; Phase and reactance; and Power in AC.

For sinusoidal supply, V=V₀sinωt and I=I₀sin(ωt+φ); frequency f=1/T and ω=2πf. RMS values for sine waves are Vrms=V₀/√2 and Irms=I₀/√2, giving equivalent heating in a resistor. A pure resistor has voltage and current in phase. A capacitor causes current to lead voltage; an inductor causes current to lag. Capacitive reactance XC=1/(ωC); inductive reactance XL=ωL. In a series RLC circuit, resonance occurs when XL=XC.
A 230 V RMS sinusoidal supply has peak voltage V₀=230√2≈325 V.

An AC source reverses polarity periodically. Peak values describe the maximum instantaneous voltage/current; RMS values describe the equivalent DC heating effect in a resistor. For a sinusoid, RMS=peak/√2. Mains ratings are usually RMS values. Frequency is cycles per second; angular frequency ω=2πf.

In a resistor, current and voltage rise and fall together. In an ideal capacitor, current leads voltage by a quarter cycle; in an ideal inductor, current lags by a quarter cycle. Capacitive reactance decreases with frequency, while inductive reactance increases. In series RLC resonance, these reactances cancel and current is greatest for a fixed voltage.

For a pure resistor, average power=VrmsIrms. In reactive circuits, voltage and current may be out of phase, so average real power includes power factor cosφ. Energy may flow back and forth between source and capacitor/inductor even when average useful power is small.

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Electrolytic conduction; Gas discharge; and Faraday's law.

Electrolytes conduct through positive cations moving to the cathode and negative anions to the anode. Electrolysis may deposit metal, release gas or change electrolyte composition. Faraday’s laws relate deposited mass to charge: m∝Q=It; m=(MIt)/(zF), where M is molar mass, z ionic charge number and F≈9.65×10⁴ C mol⁻¹. Gas conduction requires ionization by high voltage, radiation or heat; electrons and ions carry charge. A discharge tube shows conduction under suitable pressure and voltage.
A current of 2 A flows for 5 min through an electrolyte. Charge passed Q=It=2×300=600 C.

When an ionic substance is molten or dissolved in water, ions are mobile and carry current. Positive ions migrate to the cathode and are reduced; negative ions migrate to the anode and are oxidized. The chemical products depend on ion discharge preference, concentration, electrode material and whether the electrolyte is aqueous or molten.

A gas is normally a poor conductor because it has few free charge carriers. Ionizing radiation, high temperature or a strong electric field can produce electrons and ions. These carriers accelerate, collide and ionize further gas molecules, creating a discharge. At low pressure, discharge tubes can show characteristic glows.

Charge passed is Q=It. The amount of product depends on charge and ionic valency: one mole of monovalent ions requires one faraday of charge; a divalent ion requires two. The Faraday constant is charge per mole of electrons. This links current, time and mass deposited.

Introductory Electronics.intro: Electronics controls current and signals using components such as diodes, transistors and sensors. Semiconductor behaviour depends on controlled doping and junctions.

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Semiconductors and junctions; Diodes and rectification; and Transistors and logic.

A semiconductor's conductivity lies between a conductor and insulator and usually increases with temperature. An n-type semiconductor has extra mobile electrons; p-type has holes as majority carriers. A p-n diode conducts readily when forward-biased and blocks most current when reverse-biased. A rectifier converts AC to pulsating DC; a smoothing capacitor reduces ripple. A transistor can act as a switch or amplifier. Logic gates (NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR) implement Boolean operations.
A bridge or full-wave rectifier uses diode paths to make load current flow in one direction on both AC half-cycles.

Pure silicon has four valence electrons and relatively few carriers at room temperature. Doping changes conductivity: donor atoms provide extra electrons in n-type material; acceptor atoms create holes in p-type material. At a p-n junction, a depletion region forms. Forward bias reduces its barrier; reverse bias widens it and permits only a small leakage current until breakdown.

A half-wave rectifier uses one diode and passes one half-cycle; a full-wave circuit uses both halves so load current has one direction. The output is pulsating DC. A capacitor across the load charges near peaks and discharges between them, reducing ripple. A regulator can further stabilize voltage.

A bipolar transistor has emitter, base and collector. A small base current can control a larger collector current, allowing switching or amplification. Digital logic treats signals as 0/1 and uses truth tables for gates. NAND and NOR are universal because combinations can reproduce other logic operations.

Elementary Modern Physics.intro: Modern physics explains matter and radiation using quantized energy, photons, wave-particle behaviour and nuclear structure.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Photons and the photoelectric effect; Atomic energy levels; and Nuclear and particle scales.

Photon energy E=hf=hc/λ. The photoelectric effect occurs when photons eject electrons from a material; emission requires frequency above threshold and maximum kinetic energy Kmax=hf−φ, where φ is work function. Increasing intensity above threshold increases emitted-electron rate, not maximum energy; increasing frequency raises maximum energy. Atomic spectra arise from discrete energy-level transitions, with photon energy equal to the level difference. De Broglie wavelength λ=h/p describes matter waves.
A photon of frequency 6×10¹⁴ Hz has energy E=6.63×10⁻³⁴×6×10¹⁴≈3.98×10⁻¹⁹ J.

Light transfers energy in packets called photons. Each photon has energy hf. In the photoelectric effect, one photon transfers energy to one electron; some energy overcomes the work function and the remainder becomes kinetic energy. Below the threshold frequency, no electron is emitted regardless of light intensity in the basic model.

Electrons in atoms occupy allowed energy levels. An electron changes levels by absorbing or emitting a photon whose energy equals the difference between levels. Since only particular energy differences are allowed, atoms produce line spectra. Each element has a characteristic pattern useful for identifying it in stars and laboratory samples.

The electronvolt is convenient for atomic energy: 1 eV=1.60×10⁻¹⁹ J. De Broglie wavelength λ=h/p links particle momentum with wave behaviour. Nuclear binding energy can be estimated from mass defect using E=Δmc²; a small mass change corresponds to large energy because c² is large.

Energy and Society.intro: Energy resources power homes, transport, industry and communication. Comparing them requires looking at reliability, cost, environmental effects and energy security.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Comparing energy sources; Efficiency and conservation; and Grid and storage.

Fossil fuels are dispatchable but release greenhouse gases and pollutants. Nuclear fission provides high energy density with low operational carbon emissions but requires robust safety and waste management. Renewable sources include solar, wind, hydro, tidal, wave and geothermal; availability may vary and storage/grid integration matter. Energy efficiency reduces input needed for a service. Power is the rate of energy use; capacity factor compares actual output with maximum possible output over time.
Replacing an inefficient lamp with a lower-power lamp for the same light output reduces electrical energy use E=Pt over its lifetime.

Compare energy resources using life-cycle emissions, reliability, cost, land use, safety, availability and effects on communities. Fossil fuels are controllable but emit greenhouse gases; wind and solar have low operating emissions but variable output; hydro is dispatchable where geography and rainfall allow; nuclear provides steady low-carbon output but requires strict safety and waste management.

Efficiency means useful output divided by input. Improving insulation, efficient motors and LED lighting lowers the energy needed for the same service. Energy conservation in physics means total energy is conserved; in everyday policy, conserving energy means reducing wasteful use. Demand management and storage can help balance variable generation.

Electricity must be generated close to the time it is consumed unless stored. Batteries, pumped hydro and other storage shift energy across time; transmission networks share resources over regions. High-voltage transmission reduces current and cable losses for a given power, but needs transformers and infrastructure.

Dams and Energy Production.intro: Hydroelectric dams convert stored gravitational potential energy of water into electrical energy. Water flow turns a turbine coupled to a generator.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Energy conversion chain; Power from a water flow; and Benefits and impacts.

Potential energy released by mass m falling height h is mgh. For water flow rate Q (m³ s⁻¹), ideal power P=ρgQh; actual output is ηρgQh, where η is overall efficiency. A turbine converts fluid energy to rotation; electromagnetic induction in a generator converts rotation to electrical energy. Reservoirs can store energy and respond quickly, but dams alter ecosystems and communities and depend on rainfall and suitable geography.

Water stored high in a reservoir has gravitational potential energy. Flowing water turns a turbine; the turbine rotates a generator, where changing magnetic flux induces electrical energy. Some energy is lost to turbulence, friction, sound and electrical resistance, so output is less than the water's ideal energy decrease.

The mass flow rate is ρQ for volumetric flow Q. Each second, water loses gravitational energy at rate ρQgh; multiplying by efficiency gives electrical power. A greater head or flow rate increases available power. Seasonal drought, sedimentation and maintenance can reduce actual output.

Reservoir hydro can respond quickly to demand and provide stored energy. Dams may flood habitats and settlements, block fish migration, change sediment transport and alter downstream ecosystems. Small run-of-river schemes have different impacts but less storage. Assessment should include construction and community effects.

Nuclear Energy.intro: Nuclear energy comes from changes in atomic nuclei. Fission splits a heavy nucleus; fusion combines light nuclei. Both can release energy because products have greater binding energy per nucleon.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Fission and chain reactions; Radioactive decay; and Fusion and mass defect.

Mass-energy equivalence E=Δmc². In fission, a neutron triggers splitting of a heavy nucleus and further neutrons may sustain a chain reaction. A reactor controls the chain with fuel, moderator, control rods, coolant and shielding. Fusion powers stars and requires extreme temperature and confinement on Earth. Radioactive decay is random for individual nuclei but predictable statistically: N=N₀(½)^(t/T½). Ionizing radiation can damage tissue; exposure depends on activity, distance, time and shielding.
A sample with half-life 8 days has 80 mg initially. After 24 days (three half-lives), mass remaining=80×(½)³=10 mg.

blocks.x: A heavy nucleus can split after absorbing a neutron, releasing energy and additional neutrons. If on average at least one emitted neutron causes another fission, a chain reaction is sustained. A reactor controls neutron population: fuel fissions, moderator slows neutrons in many designs, control rods absorb neutrons, coolant carries heat, and shielding reduces radiation exposure.

Radioactive decay is spontaneous and random for individual nuclei. Half-life is the time for half the unstable nuclei in a large sample to decay. Activity A is decays per second and also falls by half each half-life. Isotopes with short half-lives are more active per amount but disappear faster; long-lived materials persist.

Fusion joins light nuclei and powers stars. It requires extremely high temperatures and confinement because positive nuclei repel. In both fission and fusion, products have slightly lower mass than reactants; the mass difference becomes energy, E=mc². Binding energy per nucleon helps explain why nuclei near iron are especially stable.

Solar Energy.intro: Solar radiation can be converted to useful heat or electricity. The resource is renewable but varies with time, weather, location and panel orientation.

blocks.x: Chapter map: how the ideas connect

This lesson moves from the basic model to its important applications. First understand the definitions, then connect them to the laws and worked examples. The three focused subtopics are: Photovoltaic conversion; Solar thermal systems; and Sizing and real output.

Solar thermal collectors absorb radiation to heat a working fluid. Photovoltaic cells convert light directly into electrical energy through semiconductor effects. Electrical output depends on irradiance, illuminated area, orientation, temperature and conversion efficiency. Solar energy can be stored as heat, in batteries or through other energy systems. A panel's rated peak power assumes specified test conditions; actual daily energy is power integrated over time and is usually below rated power multiplied by 24 h.
A 200 W panel operating at full rated output for 5 h would generate 1.0 kWh; real output is lower if sunlight is weak or conditions are not ideal.

A photovoltaic cell is a semiconductor junction. Absorbed photons create electron-hole pairs; the built-in electric field separates charges and drives current through an external circuit. Cells are connected in series to raise voltage and in parallel to raise current. Shading one part of a series string can reduce output substantially.

A solar thermal collector absorbs sunlight and transfers heat to water or another fluid. A dark, selective absorber and transparent cover can reduce losses; insulation behind the absorber limits conduction. Concentrating collectors focus sunlight and are most effective under direct sunshine, while flat panels also use diffuse light.

Daily electrical energy depends on panel rating, equivalent full-sun hours, orientation, shading, temperature, inverter losses and battery/charging efficiency. Rated peak power is measured under standard test conditions and is not guaranteed for every hour. Batteries store energy but add cost, losses and replacement needs.
